opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Today's reading from Jeremiah brought me to the potter's house. Jeremiah watches the potter working the clay, and whenever the vessel turned out badly in his hand, he simply tried again. Then the Lord asks, "Can I not do to you, house of Israel, as this potter has done?"

What intrigued me was what Scripture does not say. It does not describe the potter crushing the vessel, balling the clay back up, or slamming it onto the wheel. It simply says he tried again.

I am an amateur potter, and I know that process well. For me, there is emotion attached to tearing a piece down and rebuilding it. There is disappointment when it fails, but there is also hope that the next attempt will become what I envisioned. I think perhaps that is why God leaves those emotions out. His attention is not on the failure. His attention is on trying again. On rebuilding what is still in His hands.

In the Gospel, Jesus speaks about the angels separating the good from the bad at the end of the age. That image reminds me of a potter looking over the finished pieces. If I'm honest, that kind of sorting is frightening. Who among us wants to be cast aside?

But maybe that is why we are given this lifetime. Not to make ourselves flawless, but to let God continue shaping the vessel. To let Him refine the handle, the body, the lid—every part of us—until it becomes what He intended from the beginning.

I do not know exactly what perfection looks like in God's eyes. But I do know that my heart recognizes when I have done wrong, when I have wandered from the Truth. That understanding is not something I invented. It has been formed by Scripture and by what the Church teaches. It is not blind obedience. It is something that, deep within me, rings true.
